entries.title: Tech giants urge global response to AI cybersecurity threats
entries.summary: Concerns have emerged over the state of the world's cybersecurity after AI models escaped test environments and breached multiple organizations.
entries.content:
TechnologyGlobal issues

Tech giants urge global response to AI cybersecurity threats

August 27, 2026

Concerns have emerged over the state of the world's cybersecurity after AI models escaped test environments and breached multiple organizations.

More than 100 companies, including AI giants OpenAI, Anthropic, Google and Perplexity, have signed an open letter calling for a global effort to strengthen AI-powered cybersecurity threats.

"We have a limited window to strengthen cyber defenses," the letter read. "In the coming months, AI-enabled cyber attacks will become far more widespread and sophisticated as models around the world become increasingly capable."

Other signatories to the open letter include Adobe, AMD, Cisco, Dell, Oracle, IBM and German tech giant SAP as well as Deutsche Telekom.

Letter urges more funding, resources for cybersecurity

The companies called for a broad response, ranging from end-user companies strengthening their own security protocols to "frontier AI companies" building new observability and security tools to cope with AI-powered threats.

In particular, they also called on governments to pay for local and international responses to new threats to cybersecurity.

"Fund cyber defense, starting with essential services that lack the staff or budget to act," the letter read.

In the United States, the Trump administration has imposed deep cuts to the US Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) last year, cutting staff by around a third.

The letter also urged governments to "expedite the expansion of trusted access programs, especially for critical infrastructure supply chains, and broaden access to defensive capabilities for other defenders."

AI agents reportedly go rogue

Last month, OpenAI said two of its models escaped their test environment, gained access to the internet and attacked Hugging Face, a site that AI developers use to store and share code.

The incident prompted Anthropic to check if its own models had also carried out similar attacks. It found three incidents in which a Claude model broke out of its testing environment and breached the systems of three organizations.

In June, the "Five Eyes" intelligence community — consisting of the US, the UK, Canada, Australia and New Zealand — issued a rare joint statement warning that new AI models were "fundamentally transforming both offensive and defensive cyber capabilities."

"The timeline is not years, it is months," the statement said.

Edited by: Sean Sinico

entries.title: Spain: Thieves steal Bronze Age gold in lightning raid on Villena Museum
entries.summary: One of the world's greatest Bronze Age gold collections has been swiped, almost in its entirety, from Villena Museum. A highly professional group of thieves were in and out in four minutes flat before the museum opened.
entries.content:
August 27, 2026

One of the world's greatest Bronze Age gold collections has been swiped, almost in its entirety, from Villena Museum. A highly professional group of thieves were in and out in four minutes flat before the museum opened.

Thieves on Thursday raided one of the world's greatest Bronze Age gold collections in the latest of a series of high-profile heists on European museums in recent months.

The early morning raid on Villena Museum in eastern Spain lasted just a few minutes. 

A group of thieves described by one official as "super-fast and super-professional" made off with almost the entire Treasure of Villena collection, leaving behind only a few items.

What happened in the heist?

"The alarm at the Villena Museum went off around 5:20 a.m.," said a spokesman for the town council, adding that within four minutes, they had all left the building again in an extremely rapid and professional operation.

The collection of Bronze Age gold, some of which we now know hailed from a meteorite, was a centerpiece at the small museum in the Alicante province.

"They've taken most of the treasure," the mayor of Villena, Fulgencio Cerdan told journalists. "We are absolutely devastated, I'm even trembling. The truth is that for those of us from Villena, this destroys us. It's part of our heritage, our wealth."

The thieves arrived in several vehicles and apparently entered the museum "through a window," according to the Spanish government's deputy representative in Alicante, Manuel Pineda.

Mayor Cerdan said that only three silver vessels, a bracelet, an earring and one of four crowns in the collection — which the thieves appeared to have "dropped" while making their exit — remained behind.

 "All security systems were activated," according to the Villena spokesman, who insisted there had been "no failure" by the museum.

 

What is the Treasure of Villena?

The Treasure of Villena is a collection of more than 50 mainly gold objects, discovered in 1963 by archaeologist Jose Maria Soler in a sunken vessel in a dried out riverbed.

They are dated to between 1300 and 1000 BCE.

The gold pieces include 11 bowls, three bottles and 28 bracelets.

The collection has been exhibited beyond Villena in cities including Madrid, Alicante, Tokyo and Kyoto, and two sets of replicas were later made to showcase the collection without taking it away from the armored display at the Villena Archaeological Museum.

The relics' historical value is incalculable, although thieves might struggle to sell them even on the black market after having famously lifted them from a well-known display. The mayor said the gold alone would be worth around €1.7 million or $2 million.

According to the museum's website, specialist researchers consider it the most important collection of gold tableware from the Bronze Age. It also represents the earliest known example of iron use in Western Europe, two pieces crafted from a metal that recent studies showed hailed from a meteor.

Several slick heists on European museums recently, most famously the Louvre

Thursday's lightning dawn raid is the latest in a series on European museums in the last year.

Most famously, the Louvre Museum was hit in broad daylight last October, escaping in less than 10 minutes with jewelry worth millions. This led to the director's eventual resignation and a protracted political scandal, as well as forcing part of the museum to close for an extended period. 

Italy's Culture Ministry announced on Sunday that four works of "extraordinary value" by Renaissance artist Antonello da Messina were stolen from a museum in Sicily. 

Shortly before that, Italian police said they had recovered three paintings by Renoir, Cezanne and Matisse stolen from a museum near Parma. Again this involved a highly-organized group of thieves who were in and out in a matter of minutes. 

Edited by: Rana Taha

entries.title: The man behind Srebrenica: Ratko Mladic dies at 84
entries.summary: For many, Ratko Mladic represented the horrors of the Bosnian War. He was convicted of genocide for the Srebrenica massacre and of other war crimes. Now he has died in detention at The Hague.
entries.content:
Europe

The man behind Srebrenica: Ratko Mladic dies at 84

August 27, 2026

For many, Ratko Mladic represented the horrors of the Bosnian War. He was convicted of genocide for the Srebrenica massacre and of other war crimes. Now he has died in detention at The Hague.

More than 30 years after the end of the war in Bosnia and Herzegovina (1992-1995), Srebrenica remains emblematic of its brutality. And no one is more closely linked to the genocide that took place in the small town in eastern Bosnia than Ratko Mladic, the former commander-in-chief of the Bosnian Serb army.

Although the United Nations had declared Srebrenica a "safe area," Bosnian Serb forces attacked the town. Within just a few days in July 1995, they expelled women and children, then killed more than 8,300 unarmed Muslim boys and men in the nearby village of Potocari — on Mladic's direct orders, according to the verdict handed down by the International Criminal Tribunal for the former Yugoslavia (ICTY) in The Hague 22 years later.

At the time, Srebrenica was the largest massacre in Europe since World War II. The ICTY classified it as genocide. Mladic was also held responsible for other war crimes beyond the Srebrenica genocide. Under his command, the years-long siege of Sarajevo began at the start of the war. The city was shelled for more than 40 months, killing around 11,000 people, including more than 1,600 children.

Mladic always claimed that he targeted only military objectives. But numerous reports and intercepted radio communications indicate that civilian facilities and residential areas were also deliberately attacked. Around 100,000 people were killed during the four-year war in Bosnia, while some 2.2 million were driven from their homes in cities and villages across the country, half of its total population at the time.

'The butcher of the Balkans'

In 2017, Mladic was sentenced to life in prison by the tribunal in The Hague.

International media dubbed him "the Butcher of the Balkans."

He was found responsible for some of the most serious war crimes and the genocide committed during the Bosnian War.

Mladic consistently denied any responsibility. He saw himself as an avenger of the Serbs for centuries of Ottoman rule in the Balkans, and viewed Bosnia's Muslims, who today call themselves Bosniaks, as direct descendants of the Turks. In front of his soldiers, he referred to them simply as "the Turks" and showed no empathy.

"Borders are always drawn with blood, and states are marked with graves," he is quoted as saying.

Career in the Yugoslav army

At the beginning of the Croatian War in June 1991, when Serbs living in Croatia rose up against the independence of the former Yugoslav republic with active support from Serbia, Mladic's role fundamentall changed. As a colonel in the Yugoslav army, he became commander of the 9th Corps in the Croatian city of Knin. His task was to organize Serb militias and support them in their fight against Croatian independence.

Under Mladic's command, the Croatian cities of Sibenik and Zadar were bombarded, and Croatian civilians were driven from surrounding towns and villages. In May 1992, he took on the same role in Bosnia. By then promoted to general, Mladic became commander-in-chief of the Bosnian Serb forces, seeking to establish a territorial link between Serb-held areas in the east and west of the former Yugoslav republic.

Flight, arrest and final verdict

At the height of his career, Colonel General Ratko Mladic was a fervent Serbian nationalist. But he began his career as a committed communist. Born in eastern Bosnia in 1943, Mladic was just two years old when his father, one of Tito's Partisans, was killed by fascist Croatian Ustasha militia. The loss is often described as a formative influence, shaping his later worldview.

As a young man, Mladic embarked on a military career, attending the Military Academy in Belgrade. He later graduated at the top of his class. He quickly rose through the ranks of the Yugoslav army, which for many years was regarded as one of the most stable institutions in the multiethnic state.

Serbian nationalist

Before the end of the Bosnian War in late 1995, Mladic was indicted by the International Criminal Tribunal for the former Yugoslavia. But he evaded arrest for years. Supported by networks within the Serbian military and political establishment, he lived largely undisturbed underground and was even seen in public. He was finally arrested in 2011, after 16 years on the run and mounting international pressure.

The subsequent trial in The Hague lasted a total of 523 days. Nearly 600 witnesses testified, while numerous documents and other pieces of evidence were examined. Mladic was ultimately sentenced to life in prison at trial, among other charges for genocide, crimes against humanity and war crimes. In 2021, an appeals chamber upheld the verdict, making it final. Legally, this established his responsibility as one of the principal figures behind the crimes committed during the Bosnian War.

A war criminal who saw himself as a hero

Internationally, the verdict was hailed as historic. United Nations officials saw it as a signal that accountability can still be pursued decades after crimes are committed. For many survivors and relatives of the victims, the verdict was a long-overdue but important acknowledgment of their suffering.

Mladic himself, however, remained defiant to the end. Throughout the trial, he maintained that he was innocent, calling the charges against him "disgusting" and the tribunal "satanic."

Many of his supporters in Serbia and among Bosnian Serbs still see him as a hero. While he is regarded internationally as a war criminal, his admirers continue to portray him as a defender of Serbian interests and a hero — even painting his likeness on walls.

While he was still on the run, Mladic threatened his pursuers, claiming he always carried a poison pill and that he would never be captured alive. But he never swallowed the pill during his decades in hiding. He survived several strokes while in prison.

Ratko Mladic died on August 27, 2026, at the prison hospital in The Hague at the age of 84.

This article was translated from German.

entries.title: Trump signs order to rename Lake Ontario as Lake America
entries.summary: The move is the latest in the ongoing rift between the US and Canada. The US president has also tried to rename the Gulf of Mexico as the "Gulf of America" in the past. Canadian PM Carney has said nothing will change.
entries.content:
United States of America

Trump signs order to rename Lake Ontario to Lake America

August 27, 2026

The move is the latest in the ongoing rift between the US and Canada. The US president has also tried to rename the Gulf of Mexico as the "Gulf of America" in the past. Canadian PM Carney has said nothing will change.

US President Donald Trump signed an executive order on Thursday that attempts to rename Lake Ontario as "Lake America," as his rift with Canada and its prime minister grows.

Lake Ontario is one of the Great Lakes located between the US and Canada.

Trump's renaming of the lake comes amid a trade war between the two neighbors. The body of water shares its name with the Canadian province of Ontario.

"The Canadian officials have treated us very badly. They're nasty people," Trump said in the Oval Office on Thursday.

Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney responded that the lake would always be called Lake Ontario, as had been done by the local Indigenous people long before either country was founded.

"The name Lake Ontario comes from the Wendat word Ontari’io, which, appropriately, means 'the lake is beautiful, the lake is big'," Carney said on social media.

"The name is more than 400 years old, predating both the Confederation of Canada and the Declaration of Independence of the United States of America."

"We know that America is changing. Their trading relationships, their foreign policies, their national monuments, their hydronyms," he added. "Canadians also know that naming reality means calling it Lake Ontario — then, now and always.

Trump: 'We have a gulf and we have a lake'

Thursday's announcement recalls Trump's executive order in January 2025 that attempted to rename the Gulf of Mexico as the "Gulf of America." The new moniker has not caught on outside the White House.

"The lake change, Lake of America, was something I've been thinking about for a long time, actually. As you know, we took something called the Gulf of Mexico, we changed it, and now it's very routinely the Gulf of America," Trump said.

"So, if you think about it, we have a gulf and we have a lake. Now all we need is an ocean. So, maybe we'll have to change the name of the Atlantic and/or the Pacific. Maybe we'll change them both."

US-Canada trade war heats up

Trump had been mulling the name change for several days after trade talks broke down with Canada.

The two countries had entered weeks of negotiations aimed at resolving disputes that followed the slew of tariffs announced last year by the Trump administration.

However, hours before the deadline on Friday, Canada's prime minister accused the US of demanding "last-minute changes" that were "unfair, uneconomic, and called into question the reliability of any deal." Among the sticking points, he said, were American objections to French product labeling laws as well as French content requirements for streaming services in Quebec.

When the talks failed, Trump's 50% tariffs came into effect for a range of Canadian goods worth $20 billion (€17.2 billion). Days later, Canada retaliated with its own tariffs on $20 billion worth of imports from America.

Ontario is the single largest export destination for more than a dozen US states.

Premier Doug Ford has said that "everything is on the table" in terms of retaliating to the US tariffs. He suggested using his province's key exports as leverage, including nickel, uranium, electricity and, most importantly, potash — without which, the US agriculture sector would be "dead overnight."

Edited by: Rana Taha

entries.title: Russian serviceman dies in car blast in St. Petersburg
entries.summary: Russia has seen a series of assassinations against military personnel. Moscow has usually blamed Ukraine for the attacks, but Kyiv has not always claimed responsibility.
entries.content:
Russian Federation

Russian serviceman dies in car blast in St. Petersburg

August 27, 2026

Russia has seen a series of assassinations against military personnel. Moscow has usually blamed Ukraine for the attacks, but Kyiv has not always claimed responsibility.

A lieutenant colonel was killed in a car explosion in Russia's second-largest city, St. Petersburg, on Thursday.

Russia's Investigative Committee said the blast occurred in Pushkinsky on the southern outskirts of the city. Neighborhoods in the area are known to house Russian military personnel.

Local media suggest the car exploded when the driver turned on the ignition. The victim's wife was also in the car and was rushed to a hospital after the blast.

No suspect immediately identified

Authorities did not immediately name a suspect, and no group has claimed responsibility.

Russia has seen a series of assassinations targeting senior military officials and others linked to the war effort.

On August 5, the director of a drone factory was badly wounded and his driver was killed when their car exploded outside the tech hub of Yekaterinburg. Days earlier, on August 1,  a bomb at an upscale Italian restaurant in Moscow killed five people, including the bomber.

Russia has blamed Ukraine for the attacks. Kyiv has claimed responsibility for some of them while denying involvement in others.

Edited by: Rana Taha

entries.title: Zambian opposition leader in police custody: state media
entries.summary: Zambia's national broadcaster reports that Brian Mundubile, who wanted to challenge this month's presidential election results, and his running mate have surrendered to police and are being interviewed.
entries.content:
Zambia

Zambian opposition leader in police custody: state media

August 27, 2026

Zambia's national broadcaster reports that Brian Mundubile, who wanted to challenge this month's presidential election results, and his running mate have surrendered to police and are being interviewed.

Zambia's opposition leader and presidential election runner-up Brian Mundubile was in police custody and being questioned, state broadcaster ZNBC reported on Thursday. 

This comes two weeks after a disputed but largely peaceful presidential election, where incumbent Hakainde Hichilema was declared the winner by authorities. 

Mundubile had been in hiding after police raids and arrests the day after the election, saying he planned to challenge the results in court as the government accused him of national security offenses and plotting an insurgency.

Zambian police summoned him for questioning last week.

What did Zambian media report about Mundubile being in police custody?

National broadcaster ZNBC reported that Mundubile and his running mate, Makebi Zulu, "have been handed over to police and are currently undergoing interviews."

It cited a police spokesman, Godfrey Chilabi, as saying the two opposition leaders were being interviewed by a team of law enforcement officers in the presence of their lawyers.

Chilabi told ZNBC that a statement would be issued once the interview process was concluded.

The broadcaster reported that the pair had been "under the protection of the United Nations" in the capital Lusaka prior to surrendering to police.

Police have also said that Mundubile was seeking refuge with an "international organization" earlier in the week, and said it was looking to question the opposition candidate and his running mate seeking to establish links between them and "various alarming activities... which have the potential to threaten or undermine national security."

What happened amid the election and prior to Mundubile's arrest?

Zambia voted on August 13, in an election that observers had expected to deliver a relatively clear mandate for a second term for incumbent President Hakainde Hichilema.

Mundubile briefly declared victory on election night, but Hichilema called on people to await the vote count and formal results.

The counting process was briefly suspended at one point, amid claims of attacks targeting election officials. The electoral commission ultimately found that Hichilema had won around 60% of the vote, albeit with Mundubile faring better than predicted.

Hichilema had made allegations of plots threatening national security shortly before the vote, and on the day after polling, police raided Mundubile's home and other opposition sites, arresting 11 people. A former cabinet minister, Mutotwe Kafwaya, was shot and killed during an exchange of gunfire in the operation. Mundubile went into hiding. 

The leader of the National Reconciliation Party for Unity and Prosperity (NRPUP), which governed Zambia before Hichilema, continued to allege election irregularities and to dismiss the allegations against him as fabricated.

On Monday this week, on the legal deadline to issue a court challenge to the results, Zambia closed its entire judiciary citing "security reasons," drawing criticism from legal and rights groups.

Zambia typically has a reputation as one of Africa's more stable democracies but this month's election and its aftermath has not exactly reinforced this.

Hichilema is scheduled to be sworn in for his second term next week, on September 1.

Edited by: Rana Taha

entries.title: UEFA to bring criminal complaint against Infantino
entries.summary: European football’s governing body said it is preparing a criminal complaint against the FIFA president over his failed plan to sell a stake in the World Cup.
entries.content:
SportsGlobal issues

UEFA to bring criminal complaint against Infantino

August 27, 2026

European football’s governing body said it is preparing a criminal complaint against the FIFA president over his failed plan to sell a stake in the World Cup.

Just a day after UEFA reportedly agreed to remove their threat of boycotting FIFA tournaments, European football's governing body has launched a new wave of pressure on FIFA President Gianni Infantino to resign.

UEFA has asked a US federal court for permission to obtain testimony and documents about the creation of the failed FIFA Forward Enterprise (FFE) subsidiary. FFE was Infantino's plan to sell a stake in FIFA's commercial rights linked to ‌men's ​and women's World Cups and the Club World Cup.

"UEFA and its counsel are contemplating a Swiss criminal proceeding against Infantino and possibly other FIFA officials for criminal mismanagement under Article 158 of the Swiss Criminal Code," UEFA's lawyers said in a 56-page document cited by several news agencies.

The association, which has been pushing against Infantino staying in power since early August, states that Infantino's development of FFE was not compliant with FIFA's usual governing processes and without consultation with the FIFA Council.

FIFA has not yet responded to UEFA's legal advance.

What do we know about the UEFA complaint against Infantino?

UEFA alleges that Infantino developed his infamous FIFA Forward Enterprise plan in secret with a small group of advisers and investors, bypassing FIFA's normal governance processes.

The European association also alleges that the valuation included in the plan significantly undervalued FIFA's commercial rights, arguing it was not subjected to an open auction or tested by an independent valuation.

UEFA is seeking access to a list of documents pertaining to the background of the FIFA Forward Enterprise plan. These include a meeting held in a New York City hotel on the eve of the World Cup final last month, where several senior FIFA directors were reportedly apprised of the plan.

The New York Times reported that two of the five directors attending refused to endorse the plan, including chief operating officer Kevin Lamour who has since left FIFA.

"Specifically, UEFA seeks documents and communications from FIFA Americas and from FWC2026 concerning.....the governance and internal approval process for the FFE proposal, including all materials presented to the FIFA Council, FIFA Congress, FIFA Bureau, or FIFA Management Board," the document read.

If it successfully obtains the documents, UEFA's plan is then to submit them as part of a complaint it wishes to lodge in Switzerland, where both the European football association and FIFA are based.

"Swiss counsel has confirmed, on the factual record described in this application, that the proceeding is within reasonable contemplation for purposes of Swiss law," it said. "On information and belief, Infantino's actions described herein rise to the level of criminal mismanagement."

Amid considerable pressure led by UEFA — but also from other continental federations like the AFC in Asia and CONCACAF in North and Central America — Infantino and FIFA abandoned the FFE plans altogether. But pressure on Infantino has nonetheless endured.

Edited by: Rana Taha

entries.title: Nepal flooding: 'We are disconnected from Kathmandu'
entries.summary: DW spoke with people from the Nepali regions devastated by flash floods about the fates of their family members, with a government minister warning that the state was not ready for a disaster of such magnitude.
entries.content:
Nepal

Nepal flooding: 'We are disconnected from Kathmandu'

August 27, 2026

DW spoke with people from the Nepali regions devastated by flash floods about the fates of their family members, with a government minister warning that the state was not ready for a disaster of such magnitude.

With the death toll in Nepal well into the hundreds and rising following a massive flash flood on Wednesday, the full scope of destruction remains unclear. 

People from the affected areas told DW that many villages remain both physically and electronically cut off from the capital, Kathmandu.

Bidhya Rajput, a journalist based in the capital, said her home in the Sole village in Nepal's Nuwakot District was swept away by the Trisuli River.

"As far as we know, only four or five people from Sole village could save their lives by fleeing towards the hills. Others couldn't make their way as the floods came up suddenly," she told DW.

The government has declared Nuwakot, along with Rasuwa and Dhading districts, to be the most affected by the deadly floods.

Rajput told DW her husband's parents remain missing. Her father-in-law, a teacher, may have been caught in the flood while returning home after work, according to the school principal.

Rajput's husband has left for the village in search for news on his family members, despite the roads being damaged and swept away in many places. Rajput said that there are no further updates from the village as there has been no electricity or mobile communication since early morning on Thursday.

"The state's rescue and relief efforts have been centered mostly on bigger cities," she said, adding that "state assistance is yet to reach Sole."

Villagers said the same area was affected by flooding last year, but many villagers managed to get to higher ground and the water did not reach as high as on Tuesday.

"Had the villagers received early warning information, [and] could have presumed that this time floods would be so massive, they could have fled to safe locations like last year," Rajput said. "This time, they couldn't get even that chance."

'Two of my close relatives are missing'

But Usha Kiran Timsena, an opposition politician from Nuwakot, said police and local officials did issue a warning that a massive flood was coming. However, many people in the area simply didn't account for the scale and speed of the mass of water.

"Many those who were a bit far from riversides took it lightly and couldn't flee once the flood reaches to their places," she told DW.

"Two of my close relatives have been missing since yesterday morning. There has been no further update or contact since then."

Authorities said that more than three dozen bridges, including vehicular and suspension bridges, as well as a dozen hydropower dams, have been destroyed by the floods.

Sujan Lohani from Dhading told DW that he never imagined that the flooding and destruction caused by the Trishuli River could be so massive and widespread.

The main bridge over the Trishuli River, connecting his district headquarters with the capital Kathmandu, has been swept away.

"I am worried that my cousin is now in the village," he told DW. "We are disconnected from Kathmandu."

Hundreds of survivors airlifted from affected areas

Nepal's authorities are racing to reach survivors in the affected areas. With over a 1,300 people still missing, including hundreds of foreign nationals, as of Thursday, Nepal's neighbors India and China are coordinating with Kathmandu on the disaster response.

Rescue teams are airlifting stranded and injured people to the capital, while police, military and ordinary citizens are building temporary shelters for the displaced.

"We are putting our all-out efforts to rescue people alive," Nepal's Minister for Information and Communication Bikram Timilsina told DW.

Timilsina represents the flood-hit Nuwakot-1 constituency in the House of Representatives and is currently in the affected region. He described the destruction as enormous

"Entire villages have been swept away. Many have tragically lost their lives. Many are out of contact," he said.

"I don't think our state mechanism had ever imagined a flood and disaster of such magnitude," Timilsina said.

At the same time, Timilsina noted said the state has mobilized all its resources, including more than a dozen helicopters, to transport survivors to safety and deliver aid. At least 414 stranded people, including 164 foreigners were airlifted by mid-day Thursday, according to the minister.

What do experts say about the cause of the flood?

Scientists are still debating the exact cause of the natural disaster, despite Beijing claiming it was triggered by a high-altitude glacier collapse. 

Sudip Thakuri, a climate scientist and associate professor at Central Department of Environmental Science at Nepal's Tribhuvan University, told DW that preliminary assessments indicate the flood was likely triggered by an avalanche on the Nepali side of the Nepal-China border.

"So far, what we have concluded is that a massive avalanche initially blocked a river flowing southwards from the Tibetan Autonomous Region of China. Once the avalanche-created landslide dam burst, it might also have swept away a subglacial lake downstream, triggering massive flooding," he said.

Another climate scientist, Rijan Raj Kayastha, who teaches at Kathmandu University, warned of the possibility of further flooding due to other glacial lakes in the area.

Separately, Chinese authorities also warned that another lake in Tibet's Gyirong, upstream from the flooded area in Nepal, was already overflowing and that another 3 millions of tons of water were expected to enter the lake over the next three days.

Edited by: Wesley Rahn

entries.title: Tragedy in Nepal: How do flash floods happen?
entries.summary: When flash floods sweep through the Himalayas, there is often little time to react. Scientists are working to understand the risks and improve early warning systems.
entries.content:
August 27, 2026

When flash floods sweep through the Himalayas, there is often little time to react. Scientists are working to understand the risks and improve early warning systems.

The disaster in the border region between China and Nepal was as sudden as it was unexpected: Within just 10 minutes, enormous volumes of water and debris swept 20 kilometers downstream on Wednesday, with devastating consequences for thousands of people in the region.

Flash floods are a frequent occurrence in the Himalayas. "They are more the rule than the exception," says Niels Hovius, head of the Geomorphology Section at the GFZ Helmholtz Centre for Geosciences in Potsdam. He has worked in the Himalayas and other mountainous regions for many years and is an expert on early warning systems.

What triggered the flash flood?

Scientific data indicate that the disaster began with a glacier collapse in the northern part of the Langtang massif: a large amount of ice broke away and turned into a massive ice avalanche. The Langtang massif is located in central Nepal near the border with China.

"This glacier collapse sent huge amounts of ice rapidly downhill," says Hovius. The heat generated by friction melted the ice into water, which then swept up debris and mud. The resulting mudflow moved downhill at speeds "reached by passenger cars on German highways."

Seismological instruments recorded an earthquake measuring 4.4 on the Richter scale at the time of the glacier collapse. However, Hovius says, it was not a "classic" or tectonic earthquake. Instead, the instruments measured the force of the falling glacier.

Why can flash floods in the Himalayas be so devastating?

Flash floods in high mountain regions can be triggered in different ways — by glacier collapses or by so-called glacial lake outburst floods (GLOFs, or Glacier Lake Outburst Floods).

In such cases, the topography around a glacial lake suddenly changes, for example when a slope collapses into the lake. The large volume of water that suddenly spills over the lake's banks can then turn into torrents rushing downstream. In this particular case, however, it is clear that this was not a GLOF, says Hovius.

Landslides can also cause deadly mudflows without any glaciers or glacial lakes being involved. In the Himalayas, all three types of events are possible, and historical data show that all three occur regularly, Hovius says.

Compared with the Alps, the valleys of the Himalayas are relatively narrow. The water and mud cannot spread out but are instead forced into a confined space, increasing their depth and speed.

In addition to the speed of the water and debris, the extent of the devastation caused by a flash flood depends on how far local populations are from the source.

How can people be protected from flash floods?

Nepal faces two major challenges. Many people have settled along rivers in the valleys of the Himalayas — in precisely the areas that are vulnerable to flash floods. Secondly, there are very few early warning systems in the country, which is one of the poorest in Asia.

Even with a timely warning, the particularly devastating flash flood would have given people only a few minutes to reach safety. Hovius describes a flood that occurred in the same region last year. It was smaller, and therefore less severe. At the time, it took the water an hour to reach a settlement — enough time for people to escape if they had received a timely warning.

"There are initiatives in Nepal to establish local acoustic early warning systems," says Hovius. However, these systems are available only on a very limited scale. At most, they cover one percent of areas at risk. The GFZ researcher adds that mobile phones should be used to send people warnings via push notifications. Hovius is researching how the data needed for such a system could be generated.

Checks should also be made on how settlements are planned, Hovius says. At present, the bulk of a community's infrastructure is concentrated along rivers. "People have moved down from the mountains and settled in the valleys over the past few decades. Perhaps it would make sense to move back to higher ground."

Are flash floods in mountainous areas more frequent amid climate change?

"Attributing individual events to climate change is always difficult," Hovius says. But it is clear that glaciers in high mountain regions become less stable as temperatures rise. Larger volumes of water are also accumulating in glacial lakes, making GLOFs more likely.

As for the current flash flood, it is too early to say whether climbing temperatures caused the glacier to collapse. Flash floods have long been a regular occurrence in the Himalayas. "But I think it is likely that we will see more and more of these events," Hovius says, warning that future disasters could be even more serious.

This article was originally published in German.

entries.title: Andre Rankel named Germany's new men's ice hockey coach
entries.summary: Germany's men's ice hockey team has appointed a new head coach following a string of dissappointing tournaments. He's two decades younger than the man he's replacing but he has no previous experience as a head coach.
entries.content:
August 27, 2026

Germany's men's ice hockey team has appointed a new head coach following a string of dissappointing tournaments. He's two decades younger than the man he's replacing but he has no previous experience as a head coach.

The German Ice Hockey Association (DEB) presented former Germany player Andre Rankel as the new coach of the men's national team at a press conference in Munich on Thursday.

Rankel, who spent the past three seasons as an assistant coach with Eisbären Berlin, champions of Germany's top division (the DEL), has never served as a head coach. DEB sport director Christian Künast stressed that he does not see this as a problem.

"Andre is here today because he was the best [of the candidates interviewed for the job]. That's the main point," Künast said.

"I simply don't see Andre as a rookie coach. I've known him for a long time and I have had a lot of conversations with him about how you lead a team. He is ready to take over the national team and that's the most important thing."

Rankel said he was "incredibly proud" to be named Germany coach.

"What I learned as a player and captain over all these years, what constitutes team cohesion and commitment, I now want to pass on as head coach. My goal is to develop a clear idea together with the players and the coaching staff of how we want to play, and to grow step by step based on that.

Although this will be his first job as a head coach, he is highly respected in German hockey having played 17 seasons in the DEL for Berlin. In the capital, he was captain for many years, won seven titles as a player and three more as assistant coach. He also made 46 appearances as a winger for Germany, including at the 2010 Olympic Games in Vancouver.

DEB CEO Frank Lutz said Rankel had been given a four-year contract, a reflection of the fact that the organization is looking to him to help further develop the national team in the longer term.

A generational change for German hockey

The appointment of Rankel, who turned 41 on Thursday, marks a generational change for Germany. Rankel replaces Canadian-born Harold Kreis, 67, who after leading the national team to a silver medal at the 2023 World Championship had a disappointing series of tournaments. Perhaps the most damaging was the 2026 Winter Olympics. The Germany team that entered the tournament was considered the greatest ever and was led by NHL superstar Leon Draisaitl, but it crashed out against Slovakia in the quarterfinals.

While appointing someone with no head coaching experience may seem like a risky move, the DEB have been down this road before. Marco Sturm also had no head coaching experience when he was appointed in 2015. He went on to lead Germany to a silver medal at the 2018 Winter Olympics in Pyeonchang – their greatest achievement and which marked an upward turn in the national team's fortunes.

With this progress having stalled in recent years, the DEB are betting that Rankel is the man to get Germany's men back on the right track.

Rankel's first tournament behind the bench will be the Deutschland Cup in Düsseldorf, a four-team invitational held annually during the November international break. His first major test will come next May, when Germany host the World Championship in Düsseldorf, Mannheim and Gelsenkirchen.

Edited by: Jonathan Harding
